subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
verificationNote: Transcribed from 2-page university paper ID 312052; independently written conceptual solutions, not formally instructor-reviewed.

questions.question: List basic functional units of a digital computer.
questions.answer: Input, output, memory/storage, arithmetic and logic unit (ALU), control unit, and registers. The CPU includes ALU, control logic and registers; buses interconnect components.

questions.question: What are general-purpose registers?
questions.answer: Fast on-chip CPU registers used to hold temporary operands, addresses and intermediate results without a single dedicated role. Architectures expose a limited register set, such as R0…R15, subject to calling conventions and special uses.

questions.question: Explain floating-point representation.
questions.answer: A real number is represented approximately as sign × significand × base^exponent. IEEE-754 binary32 has 1 sign bit, 8 biased-exponent bits (bias 127), and 23 fraction bits; ordinary normalized numbers have an implicit leading 1. This gives large dynamic range but rounding error; special encodings represent zero, infinity and NaN.

questions.question: Role of ALU in processor.
questions.answer: The ALU performs arithmetic (add, subtract, shifts), Boolean/bitwise operations (AND, OR, XOR, NOT) and comparisons. It consumes operands from registers, outputs results to registers, and may update status flags (zero, carry, sign, overflow).

questions.question: Discuss microoperations.
questions.answer: Microoperations are elementary operations on data held in registers during a clock or control step: register transfer (R1←R2), arithmetic (R1←R1+R2), logic (R1←R1 AND R2), and shifting/rotating. A control unit orchestrates them to implement machine instructions.

questions.question: Purpose of ROM.
questions.answer: Read-only memory stores information retained without power: boot firmware, microcode or device constants. Typical ROM/flash is nonvolatile, with slower and limited rewriting compared with RAM. Firmware executes startup checks and starts the operating-system loader.

questions.question: List peripheral devices.
questions.answer: Keyboard, mouse, scanner, webcam, microphone, monitor, printer, external disks/USB storage, network adapters, speakers and industrial sensors/actuators. They exchange data with the CPU over I/O controllers/interfaces.

questions.question: Explain data transfers among registers, buses and memory, with read/write.
questions.answer: The CPU places a memory address in the Memory Address Register (MAR) and drives address lines. Read: assert memory-read control; memory returns the addressed word on the data bus into Memory Data Register (MDR); CPU transfers MDR to destination register. Write: load MAR with destination address and MDR with data; assert memory-write; memory stores MDR at MAR. Transfers are synchronized by clocks/handshaking and are mediated by the memory controller. Conceptual diagram: CPU registers ↔ internal bus ↔ MDR ↔ data bus ↔ Memory; MAR → address bus → Memory; control unit → Read/Write lines.

questions.question: Describe Booth's signed binary multiplication, advantages.
questions.answer: For n-bit two's-complement multiplicand M and multiplier Q, initialize A=0 and Q-1=0. Repeat n cycles: examine (Q0,Q-1). 01 → A=A+M; 10 → A=A−M; 00/11 → no add/subtract; then arithmetic-right-shift concatenation [A,Q,Q-1]. After n cycles [A,Q] is 2n-bit signed product. A run of 1 bits is represented by boundary operations, reducing partial additions for clustered 1s. Works directly with two's-complement signs; standard Booth may do as many operations for alternating bit patterns. Example M=3, Q=−2 yields product −6.

questions.question: Explain horizontal and vertical microprogramming.
questions.answer: Horizontal microcode uses wide control words with many direct control bits; potentially triggers multiple compatible microoperations in parallel, fast decoding but high control memory cost. Vertical microcode uses compact encoded control fields requiring decoding; saves ROM size, but reduces immediate parallelism and adds decoder latency. Hardware designs may use hybrids.

questions.question: Compare magnetic disks, tapes and optical disks as auxiliary memory.
questions.answer: Magnetic disk (HDD): rotating random-access, large capacity and good cost/GB; mechanical seek/rotation latency, vulnerable to shocks. Magnetic tape: sequential access, very high capacity and low archival cost but slow searching; used in backups and cold storage. Optical disc (CD/DVD/Blu-ray): laser reading/writing, removable media, relatively modest capacity and transfer speed; useful for distribution/archives. All are nonvolatile, unlike RAM.

questions.question: Explain I/O ports, characteristics and significance.
questions.answer: An I/O port is an addressable interface/register or physical connection between host and a device controller. Controller status, data and command registers expose device state. CPU may use memory-mapped I/O or dedicated I/O instructions; handshaking, interrupts, buffering and DMA manage different speeds. Interfaces such as USB/PCIe add protocol, bus width, timing and power characteristics, letting OS drivers exchange data reliably.

questions.question: Explain CPU organization, fetch/decode/execute, pipeline and parallelism.
questions.answer: Processor components: control unit, instruction decoder, PC, instruction register, general registers, ALU, status registers, cache and internal buses. Fetch: IR←Memory[PC]; PC advances. Decode instruction, identify operands/addressing mode. Execute through ALU, memory read/write or branch; write result and update flags/PC. A pipeline overlaps stages (e.g., IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB) for higher throughput; data, control and structural hazards require forwarding, stalls, branch prediction or resource duplication. Parallel techniques include superscalar issue, SIMD/vector units, multiple cores and simultaneous multithreading. More parallelism needs hazard checks, synchronization and coherent memory.

questions.question: Compare address bus, data bus and control bus.
questions.answer: Address bus identifies memory/I/O location; CPU typically drives it outward, width n supports up to 2^n byte addresses under a byte-addressed model. Data bus transfers instructions and data, usually bidirectional, its width affects how many bits transfer per beat. Control bus conveys signals such as read/write, clock/ready, interrupt requests, bus arbitration and reset. Example CPU fetch: address bus carries PC address, read signal travels on control bus, instruction word returns via data bus.

questions.question: Explain carry lookahead adder (CLA) vs ripple carry adder.
questions.answer: For bit i: generate G_i=A_i B_i, propagate P_i=A_i xor B_i. Carry C_(i+1)=G_i+P_i C_i. A CLA expands this relation, e.g. C2=G1+P1 G0+P1 P0 C0; many carries can be computed in parallel with logic networks. Ripple carry computes each carry after the previous one, resulting in O(n) carry delay and small area; CLA reduces delay (group lookahead often logarithmic with hierarchical designs) at cost of extra gates, wiring and fan-in.

questions.question: Explain signed operand multiplication.
questions.answer: Signed binary multiplication uses two's complement or sign-magnitude representation. For two's-complement n-bit operands, product needs up to 2n bits, with correct sign extension on partial products. Booth recoding examines adjacent multiplier bits and performs ±multiplicand followed by arithmetic shifts; it handles negative operands directly. Example 4-bit −3 is 1101, +5 is 0101, product −15 represented in 8-bit two's complement as 11110001. Preserve arithmetic right shift and enough result bits to avoid overflow.

questions.question: Describe horizontal and vertical microprogramming in control-unit design.
questions.answer: Microinstructions reside in control store; sequencer selects next address. Horizontal format allocates separate bits/groups to assert control signals directly: wide words, low decoding overhead, high parallelism and high ROM area. Vertical format encodes mutually exclusive microoperation choices in shorter fields requiring decoder logic: narrow words, lower ROM area but added decode delay. Compare along word width, control-store size, speed, parallel microoperations, ease of modification and hardware complexity; hybrid formats balance them.

questions.question: Explain microprogram sequencing for complex instructions.
questions.answer: A control-store address register (µPC/CAR) points to microinstruction in control memory. The control word activates datapath microoperations and includes next-address/branch information. Sequencer selects µPC+1, dispatch address from opcode, conditional branch based on flags or return address from micro-subroutine. For a memory ADD instruction, possible steps: fetch IR, decode/dispatch, compute effective address, memory-read operand, add to accumulator, store result, dispatch to next fetch. This makes complex ISA instructions implementable through reusable, testable sequences.

questions.question: Design and explain memory hierarchy.
questions.answer: From smallest/fastest/most expensive per bit to largest/slower/cheapest: CPU registers → L1 cache → L2/L3 cache → DRAM → SSD/HDD → archival tape/cloud. Locality drives efficiency: temporal locality reuses recent data, spatial locality accesses nearby addresses. Cache is block-based with tags and replacement policy; levels trade latency, capacity and bandwidth. Miss penalty grows with lower levels. Virtual memory uses pages and disk as backing store but is much slower than RAM.

questions.question: Describe DRAM and SRAM architecture and operation.
questions.answer: SRAM usually uses cross-coupled transistors (e.g. 6T cell) storing a stable bit while powered; very fast, no periodic refresh, larger cell/cost; used for cache. DRAM stores a bit as capacitor charge accessed by a transistor (1T1C); charge leaks, so rows require refresh; reading is destructive and needs sense-amplifier restore; denser and cheaper per bit but slower; used as main memory. Both use row/column decoders, sense/data circuitry and read/write control.

questions.question: Role of peripheral devices and their interaction through I/O interfaces.
questions.answer: Peripherals provide data input, output, storage and communications. Device controllers bridge device protocols to CPU/system bus; driver software programs command registers, transfers data through data ports or DMA, and examines status. Programmed I/O uses polling, interrupt-driven I/O lets CPU run other tasks until an event, DMA transfers large blocks with minimal per-byte CPU work. Interrupt controllers, bus arbitration, buffering and access protection enable reliable integration.

questions.question: Explain DMA techniques for data transfer.
questions.answer: DMA controller copies data directly between device controller and main memory. CPU programs device address, memory address, direction and count, then DMA arbitrates for the bus and transfers; completion usually triggers an interrupt. Modes: burst/block transfer occupies bus for a block; cycle stealing transfers one word at a time interleaved with CPU; transparent/idle-cycle DMA uses otherwise unused bus cycles. Supports scatter-gather descriptors and bus-mastering. CPU still handles setup/cache coherency and error conditions; DMA improves throughput and reduces interrupt/copy overhead.
